result.summary: Nausicaa returns home, and Minerva, disguised as a girl, guides the hidden Ulysses to the palace of Alcinous and advises him to appeal to Queen Arete. He supplicates her, is welcomed, and tells how he came from Calypso's island to Scheria. Alcinous offers an escort home and even his daughter's hand, and Ulysses is given a bed.

scenes.title: Nausicaa returns home
scenes.summary: Nausicaa reaches her father's house, where her brothers unload the mules and her old nurse Eurymedusa lights a fire.

scenes.title: Minerva guides Ulysses
scenes.summary: Hidden in mist, Ulysses meets Minerva disguised as a girl. She leads him to the palace and tells him of Arete and her family.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses risks hostility from suspicious Phaeacians and needs the queen's favour to get home.

scenes.title: Splendours of Alcinous's palace
scenes.summary: Minerva goes to Athens while Ulysses marvels at the palace, its golden dogs, maids and ever-fruiting garden.

scenes.title: Ulysses supplicates Arete
scenes.summary: Ulysses clasps Arete's knees and begs for passage home. Echeneus urges hospitality, and Alcinous promises an escort the next day.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses depends on the hospitality and goodwill of the Phaeacians to get home.

scenes.title: Ulysses tells of Calypso
scenes.summary: Arete recognises the clothes and questions him. Ulysses recounts his shipwreck, seven years with Calypso, the raft, Neptune's storm and Nausicaa's help.
scenes.stakes: Ulysses must satisfy his hosts' questions while protecting Nausicaa's name.

scenes.title: Offer of escort and a bed
scenes.summary: Alcinous offers Ulysses his daughter and a swift voyage home, and Ulysses is put to bed in the gatehouse.

notable_quotes.reason: Ulysses' memorable remark that hunger overrides sorrow.
Minerva's advice that boldness helps even a stranger.

analysis.text: Hospitality and supplication (xenia) are central: Ulysses must win protection through the proper ritual of clasping the queen's knees.
The palace and garden describe an idealised world of wealth and seafaring, reflecting Greek views of the remote, blessed Phaeacians.

legacy.text: The ever-fruiting garden of Alcinous became a classical model of the ideal garden and of paradise-like abundance.

fun_facts.text: The golden and silver dogs made by Vulcan are an early literary example of artificial, living guardians.

language_notes.text: "Comely" means good-looking or handsome; the comparison to the gods is a conventional compliment.
"Chosen as a prize" means she was picked from the spoils or captives as a special gift to the king, i.e. she was a slave.
"Father stranger" is a respectful form of address to an older man whose name is unknown.
"Cannot abide" means cannot tolerate or endure.
"To boot" means in addition, as well.
"Without male issue" means having no sons; the line passed to his daughter Arete.
Erechtheus was a legendary early king of Athens; his house stands for the Athenian palace where Minerva (the Greek Athene) was worshipped.
Cornice: the decorative moulding along the top of a wall. Blue enamel here means a dark blue glazed or glass-like material.
Lintel is the horizontal beam above a door; the hook is the door's handle or latch-ring.
Mastiffs are large, powerful guard dogs; here they are artificial, made of metal.
"Will turn oil" means the cloth is so tightly woven that oil runs off it without soaking in.
The vineyard is described as showing every stage of the grape harvest at once, from blossom to raisins and pressing.
Mercury (the Greek Hermes) was the god of sleep's messenger and guide; a last libation to him before bed was a Phaeacian custom.
Laying hands on the queen's knees was the formal gesture of a suppliant, placing himself under her protection.
Jove protects suppliants and strangers, so Echeneus invokes him to remind Alcinous of the duty of hospitality.
"Aldermen and town councillors" is the translator's English civic wording for the Phaeacian chiefs and counsellors.
Hecatombs were large sacrifices, originally of a hundred oxen, offered to the gods.
The Phaeacians claim close kinship with the gods, like the Cyclopes and Giants, who were also descended from divine stock.
"Importunate" means persistently demanding, here describing hunger.
"The hand of heaven has been laid heavy upon me" means the gods have afflicted him with suffering.
"Hearth" stands for home; being brought to her hearth means arriving at her dwelling as a guest.
"Seven years straight on end" means seven continuous years; "bade me depart" means she told or allowed him to leave.
"Days seven and ten" is archaic for seventeen days; the eighteenth day brings the first sight of land.
"Besought" in the next lines means begged; here the sense is that he pleaded humbly for help.
"Westering" means sinking toward the west, so it was late afternoon.
"By Father Jove, Minerva, and Apollo" is an oath invoking three gods to guarantee his sincerity.
Euboea is a long island off Greece's eastern coast. Rhadamanthus, a judge of the dead in later tradition, is said to have visited Tityus there, a giant son of Gaia (Earth).
"Sleep64" contains a stray footnote number from the source edition; it is not part of the text.
"Echoing gateway" describes the resounding portico or porch of the palace, where guests were commonly lodged.

context_notes.text: Minerva (the Greek Athene) is Ulysses' divine protector, and she often helps him by disguising or concealing him.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon) is god of the sea, and the Phaeacians were famed sailors under his favour.
Scheria is the island of the Phaeacians.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus) was the god of the forge and craftsmanship, famed for making marvellous metal objects.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) was goddess of wisdom and handicrafts, including weaving, which explains her gift to the Phaeacian women.
Minerva (the Greek Athene) had hidden Ulysses in mist so he could cross the city unseen to reach the palace.
Sitting in the ashes of the hearth was a suppliant's posture of humility, and the hearth was a sacred place.
Alcinous alludes to the Fates, who were thought to spin each person's destiny at birth, beyond the Phaeacians' control.
Calypso is a nymph-goddess, daughter of Atlas, who held Ulysses on her island for years, wishing him to be her husband.
Calypso offered Ulysses immortality, a great gift. He refused because he longed to return home to Ithaca and his wife.
Neptune (the Greek Poseidon), god of the sea, is angry with Ulysses for blinding his son, the Cyclops Polyphemus.
Alcinous is king of the Phaeacians; his daughter Nausicaa found Ulysses on the shore and told him to follow her cart to the palace.
Offering his daughter to a stranger shows Phaeacian generosity, though Ulysses is already married to Penelope and wants to go home.
Arete is Alcinous' queen, highly honoured among the Phaeacians, and she directs the household's hospitality.

literary_notes.text: Ulysses does not know the helpful girl is a goddess, while the reader does.
The ships are compared to thought and to a bird, stressing their supernatural speed.
Arete's wisdom and public honour are described at length, preparing readers for her key role as Ulysses' advocate.
The shuttles moving to and fro are compared to fluttering aspen leaves, giving the weaving a light, quick, shimmering motion.
Fruit that never fails in any season exaggerates the garden's abundance, marking it as a place of divine, almost unreal plenty.
The narrator steps back to sum up the description, stressing that the palace's wonders are gifts of the gods.
The darkness falling away at the moment of touching the queen's knees makes Ulysses' sudden appearance vivid and dramatic.
Hunger is given a will of its own, thrusting itself on a man's notice and overriding his grief.
Ulysses' longing for his property and household shows his deep attachment to home and his resolve to return.
Watering the clothes with tears conveys his long grief and homesickness through a vivid, concrete image.
Nausicaa "looking like a goddess" compares her beauty to the divine, flattering the princess and her family.
Ulysses praises Nausicaa's good sense beyond her years, building her character and subtly pleasing her parents.
Ulysses tactfully shields Nausicaa and flatters his host, showing his diplomatic skill.
The claim that sailors crossed the farthest known distance and back in one day boasts of Phaeacian seamanship in exaggerated terms.
Ulysses sleeps in the outer gateway while the king rests inside with his wife, ending the scene by marking his guest status and his lack of a home and spouse.
